title: “The manager made me”: why Leandro Paredes misses Boca v Riestra - OneFootball
content: Get the full live experience with the OneFootball app. The accumulated physical wear and tear of recent weeks forced Boca’s coaching staff to take precautions ahead of the start of the local competition. Paredes will not play for Boca against Riestra: “The coach forced me to take two days off”. The Xeneize captain will not be available for the Torneo Clausura opener against the Malevo at the request of Rodolfo Arruabarrena, who agreed to let him play against O’Higgins but asked him to take a breather, after the intense run of matches he faced with both the national team and the club. The holding midfielder’s commitment was recognized by the fans during the continental match played at La Bombonera. In Boca’s 1-0 win over O’Higgins in the Copa Sudamericana playoffs, Leandro Paredes showed exemplary commitment that Boca fans rewarded with a deafening ovation: four days after playing in the World Cup final with the Argentina national team, he pulled on the blue and gold and played all 90 minutes against the Chilean side. The workload the midfielder went through in recent days was extremely demanding. On Sunday, under the intense New York sun, he played 75 minutes in the World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. Physically exhausted after playing the last few matches with a cracked rib and with the disappointment of having lost — which included an outburst involving Eric García and Gavi — the next day he began the trip back to the country alongside 15 teammates, as well as club officials and members of the coaching staff. As soon as he set foot on Argentine soil, the footballer immediately rejoined the squad’s routine. On Tuesday morning he returned to training at Boca Predio and made himself available to Arruabarrena to start two days later against O’Higgins. El Vasco accepted his request, and the captain not only made the squad but started and played the full 90 minutes. The midfielder acknowledged the impact of the trip, the run of matches, and the coach’s order to stop. At the end of the match at the Alberto J. Armando stadium, the midfielder himself spoke about the effort in the mixed zone. “I’m tired. I thought I’d be feeling better, but clearly the trip, the 50 days, and all the matches I had on me take their toll. I wanted to be here, I wanted to be part of the team because the sense of belonging is huge and I always want to be here. In that sense, I’m happy because we played and we won,” Paredes said. He also explained the measure taken by the coaching staff to protect his physical condition: “I’ve lived it this way throughout my whole career, imagine what I’m willing to do for Boca. I try to give back the affection the fans show me with this kind of thing, by always being available, although now the coach forced me to take two days off because you really do feel everything the World Cup, the trip, and today’s match put you through”. Boca will open the Torneo Clausura with the confirmed absence of its captain and possible squad rotation. As a result of this technical decision, the midfielder will not take part in the next tactical sessions. The captain will follow El Vasco’s order, will not be part of Friday’s or Saturday’s training sessions and, as a result, will be left out of the squad for Sunday’s league opener against Deportivo Riestra at 7:15 p.m. at Guillermo Laza. title: BackupChain Expands Hyper-V Backup for Windows Server 2025 as a Veeam Alternative - EIN Presswire

BackupChain adds faster compression, Hyper-V change tracking, single-pass restores, and Deep Verification for Hyper-V backups on Windows Server and Windows 11. BALTIMORE, MD, UNITED STATES, July 24, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- BackupChain today announced a major update to its backup and disaster recovery platform, bringing faster compression, improved Hyper-V protection, quicker restores, and deeper backup validation to Windows Server users and SMBs. Storage is getting harder to manage. Drives cost more, data keeps growing, and businesses need to keep more backups for longer periods. BackupChain addresses these challenges with a redesigned deduplication engine that reduces storage usage while improving backup speed. The result: fewer storage headaches and lower infrastructure costs. The new release adds advanced Hyper-V change tracking to speed up incremental backups and reduce unnecessary data movement. BackupChain tracks what actually changed inside virtual machines, allowing administrators to run efficient backups without wasting time processing unchanged data. The new Hyper-V RCT Hyper-V Backup is not only available on Windows Server 2016 and later, but also to Hyper-V hosts running on Windows 10 and Windows 11. Hyper-V RCT Recovery has also become simpler with single-pass restores. When a system needs to come back online, administrators can restore data more directly instead of navigating complicated recovery workflows. Faster recovery means less downtime and fewer disruptions. Another major addition is Deep Verification for VM backups. BackupChain Hyper-V Backup now verifies the complete backup chain while operations continue, checking that virtual machine backups remain consistent and recoverable. This gives IT teams greater confidence that their backups will work when they need them most, without requiring a restoration of the virtual machine. “Backup teams do not need more complexity. They need tools that work,” said Melissa Weekley, President at FastNeuron. “We built these improvements around real-world problems: rising storage costs and growing virtual environments.” BackupChain provides businesses with a practical alternative to larger enterprise backup platforms such as Veeam. While many enterprise solutions focus on broad feature sets and complex deployments, BackupChain's Veeam alternative focuses on delivering powerful backup technology for organizations running Microsoft Windows and Hyper-V environments. The platform combines compression, virtualization support, verification technology, and flexible backup options in a solution designed for SMBs, IT professionals, and organizations that want enterprise-level protection without unnecessary overhead. With this release, BackupChain continues its mission: making reliable backup and recovery faster, more affordable, and easier to manage.The latest BackupChain version is available now. title: Section V flag football stars rack up all-state honors - Democrat and Chronicle
content: As high school flag football continues to grow in popularity, so does the number of Section V players earning recognition among the state's best. The New York State Sportswriters Association put together the first set of all-state flag football teams in 2025. This year's selections include seven players at Section V schools named first team all-state, one more than last season. Webster Schroeder quarterback Emma Rascoe has completed her high school playing days as a two-time member of the Class B all-state first team offense. Rascoe, the 2026 Democrat and Chronicle All-Greater Rochester Player of the Year, finished with 63 touchdown passes and 78 total touchdowns during her senior season as Webster Schroeder went 14-2. She finished with 4,729 all-purpose yards, including 3,776 passing yards, while helping the Warriors win the Section V Class B championship. The Warriors were state champions in 2025. Bishop Kearney standout Nela Lopusanova, a three-time AGR first team member, and East Rochester defensive star Payton Kinney earned Class C first-team all-state honors for the second consecutive year. title: Amicus Brief: StandWithUs v. MIT - Manhattan Institute
content: Don't miss the newsletters from MI and City Journal After the attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, protests happened at universities around the country. At MIT, students and faculty protesters called for violence against Jews. Protesters disrupted classes and impeded access to public spaces, and they coalesced around Jewish community and religious locations as they targeted students and faculty because of their Jewish identities. These actions, among others, violated MIT’s time, place, and manner rules for protests, and made campus life intolerable for Jews. Because MIT failed to take adequate steps to address these realities, its campus devolved into a severely antisemitic environment. StandWithUS challenged MIT's actions (or lack thereof) as a violation of its obligations under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. MIT is a private university, but it is still required to at least not be "deliberately indifferent" to a "hostile environment." The First Circuit ruled that MIT's actions were not deliberately indifferent to a hostile environment because the protesters were anti-Zionistic rather than antisemitic, and the protesters' speech was political speech protected by the First Amendment. Now on petition for Supreme Court review, the Manhattan Institute has filed a brief in support. We argue that the lower court made errors in how it interpreted the facts at the pleading stage. The First Circuit illegitimately explained away each fact rather than looking holistically at the totality of facts that created an antisemitic environment. That approach to the pleadings also highlights a circuit split about the legal standard to apply to cases like this. The Supreme Court should take the case to clarify how to apply Title VI. title: AMD EPYC “Venice” Gives Us A Preview of Zen 6-Based Ryzen “Olympic Ridge” CPUs: More Cores, More (3D V-)Cache, Clocks & Scalable Configs - Wccftech
content: AMD has launched its first Zen 6 CPUs, the EPYC Venice, and we use them to analyze what we can expect from the Ryzen "Olympic Ridge" lineup. It is surprising how AMD has evolved its strategy over the years. When the first Zen architecture launched, it was released for desktop PCs. The 1st Gen EPYC family, codenamed Naples, wouldn't arrive till a few months later. This has been the case for all Zen launches so far: Ryzen launches first, followed by EPYC, but with Zen 6, this has changed. The Zen 6-based EPYC Venice family has launched, and the Ryzen family will be launching several months later in early 2027. You can think of AI being a major factor in this decision by AMD. We've seen how big a demand there is for compute, and we have also seen how the PC segment isn't in its greatest shape at the moment due to rising component prices & stringent shortages across all sectors. So AMD's decision kind of makes sense, but despite all of that, Ryzen Desktop CPUs remain a crucial market for the chipmaker, and there are a lot of enthusiasts who are waiting to see what AMD has in store for them with the next-gen lineup. We have detailed some aspects of next-generation Ryzen CPUs, but the EPYC "Zen 6" lineup gives us even more clues to where Ryzen might be heading next. The first detail that we can confirm now is that AMD's Zen 6 will feature more cores and threads. Since AMD Zen 1 and Zen 2, the Ryzen family peaked at 8 cores and 16 threads. Each of these Zen architectures featured a single CCD (Compute Core Die), which included two CCX (Compute Core Complex). The first two generations had 16 MB of L2 cache dedicated to each CCX, so while these CCXs resided on the same CCD, they didn't have true "Share LLC". This changed with Zen 3, Zen 4, and Zen 5 generations, which transitioned to the modern-day CCD design, more full, and packing up to 16 cores with 32 threads. Each of these featured 8 cores per CCD, and since the CCX became the CCD itself, it meant that the full 32 MB cache could now be shared across the chips. So you went from 8 cores to 16 cores, & from 16 MB cache to 32 MB cache (Pre-Zen 3 Ryzens had 1 CCD with two 16 MB CCXs, whereas Zen 3 & above have two CCDs with 32 MB per die). But we have been through three generations of Zens without any major core or cache uplift. The 3D V-Cache options did bring more cache, but the core configuration got stagnant. Now with Zen 6, we will see a major change. Once again, AMD will retain the same two CCD & one IOD structure for Zen 6-based Ryzen CPUs. First of all, AMD has confirmed that Zen 6 will feature two variants: Zen 6 with 12 cores per die and Zen 6C with 16 cores per die. The Zen 6C flavor is going to be exclusive to the enterprise & HPC segment, so that gives us 12 cores per die. And the base EPYC 9016, an 8-core chip, confirms that Zen 6 has 48 MB of cache per CCD. So besides a 50% increase in core count, Zen 6 also gets a 50% increase in cache. Two Zen 6 CCDs means that the flagship Ryzen "Olympic Ridge" Desktop CPU would offer up to 24 cores, 48 threads, and 96 MB of L3 cache, while a single CCD variant will offer up to 12 cores, 24 threads, and 48 MB of L3 cache. So if we compare Zen 6 to Zen 5, we will be getting: From previous details, it is expected that Ryzen "Olympic Ridge" CPUs will scale across several SKUs with various core counts and caches: Now for the clock speeds, AMD's Zen 6 CPUs are expected to further raise the frequency ceiling, and that can be seen on many 6th Gen EPYC CPUs already. The standard Zen 6 CPUs are dialing up to 5.00 GHz, and upcoming V-Cache flavors will feature a 5.15 GHz clock. Now the comparison with EPYC CPUs isn't straightforward, as server chips have stricter power profiles & are designed with endurance/stability in mind. Desktop CPUs feature much higher clocks as they are more flexible with clocks, power (TDP/PPT), platform, and the chip itself, which shares that power budget with massive IO dies. So we compare the generational uplifts of Zen 6 "EPYC" with Zen 5 "EPYC". The maximum base clock for Zen 6 EPYC is rated at 3.90 GHz, whereas the maximum base clock for Zen 5 EPYC is rated at 3.80 GHz. The boost clocks for Zen 5 go up to 5.0 GHz, and the same is true for Zen 6, but that will change early next year when better bins arrive with 5.15 GHz clocks. On average, comparing SKUs with the same core count, we can note a 3.1% bump in base and a 3.7% bump in boost clocks. Even with a 5.15 GHz Zen 6 SKU, the boost profile is only raised by 3 percent, which is in line with the rest of the chips. If we apply the averages to the fastest chip in the Ryzen 9000 stack, we go from 5.7 GHz to just shy of 6.0 GHz. But let's do something else and apply the maximum boost uplifts that each core config up to 24 has on offer. The 8-core sees a 17% bump, which, if applied to an existing 8-Core AMD Ryzen 7 9850X3D, pushes the clock speeds beyond 6.5 GHz (from 5.6 GHz). A 16-core model goes from 5.6/5.7 GHz to 6.1/6.2 GHz (applying the 1.097x boost of the EPYC 9116), and for 24-core models, the max boost uplift of 1.11x should push boost clocks up to 6.2-6.3 GHz. Quick Side Node - AMD EPYC Venice (Zen 6 Classic) is based on N2P, whereas EPYC Turin (Zen 5 Classic) is based on N4X. For Ryzen, the Olympic Ridge (Zen 6 Classic) will feature the same N2P process node, while existing Granite Ridge (Zen 5 Classic) CPUs feature the N4P node. N4X offers a 4% performance increase over N4P. So the node itself can add an additional boost in frequency. Now that is assuming AMD guns for clock speed alone. If power is traded to other aspects of the chip, then we can see a more baseline set around 6-6.2 GHz, which should put Ryzen Zen 6 in the same league as Intel's Raptor Lake Refresh chips, which currently offer the highest clock speeds on desktops. Intel toned down its clock speeds with Arrow Lake, so we kind of wish to see some decent figures in next-gen lineups. Now for power consumption, once again, the fact that EPYC is much bigger in general and features two huge IO dies means that its power characteristics will always be higher than a standard Desktop chip, but there's also a difference in terms of power management. Servers & respective CPUs rely heavily on fast and feature-rich IO capabilities, which is why the IO dies are huge, as they are on EPYC chips. So more IO, more chiplets, more power. On Desktops, this power is managed within a lower number of chiplets, which means that more power envelope is available to the CCDs. In return, the chips can yield higher frequency or trade off that power for extra efficiency. The balance needs to be there, but Desktop and Enthusiast chips often squeeze out every bit of headroom that is available. The switch to TSMC's 2nm process also brings some nice improvements. From Zen 5 on TSMC 3nm to Zen 6 on 2nm, the power numbers see a drastic drop for each respective SKU under the same core count. Across all variants, we see an average -10% drop in power consumption. Only one SKU, the 8-core model, sees a +4% bump in power. This shows that Zen 6 is generally down in power but up in all performance vectors. So while this doesn't mean that power numbers on AMD's Ryzen "Olympic Ridge" chips will go down, it does mean that Zen 6 will provide extra power headroom to be directed to the cores & that could lead to more clocks or performance. Now for cache, we have mentioned how that is improved by 50% to 48 MB per CCD. That gets us to 96 MB on a dual CCD variant, which is the exact amount of cache as the 8-Core 3D V-Cache CPU series. This will bring a decent boost in gaming performance on non-3D V-Cache chips, but with 3D V-Cache, we can expect a bigger bump. That's because Venice-X is packing 1152 MB of L3 cache. And that gives us an idea of what the next-gen 3D V-Cache is going to offer. Venice-X is based on the classic Zen 6 cores, so that's 48 MB of L3 cache per CCD for a total of 384 MB of standard cache across eight CCDs. That means the remaining 768 MB of L3 comes from 3D V-Cache, and that number totals at 96 MB of 3D V-Cache per CCD. Current AMD Ryzen and EPYC CPUs feature up to 64 MB of 3D V-Cache. This amount was true for both the first and second generations of the technology. The second generation flipped the 3D stack beneath the CCD, and the same is true for the Zen 6 cores. But a 96 MB 3D V-Cache represents a 50% boost in X3D offerings. While current 3D V-Cache CPUs still offer more cache per CCD, which improves gaming perf, a 48 MB cache still represents a nice bump over the existing 32 MB design. This will mark the first major increase in the 3D V-Cache amount since its introduction with the Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU. So let's bring out the numbers: Now here's an interesting thing to note: Intel's Nova Lake bLLC variants with single compute tiles will feature up to 144 MB cache, while dual compute tiles will feature up to 288 MB cache. AMD's next-gen 3D V-Cache with boosted capacities will be ideally positioned with the same 144 MB on single CCD and 288 MB on dual CCD models. So if you round everything up, you can see that AMD has set up a great foundation for its next iteration of Ryzen chips, which will unpack more capabilities with the Zen 6 core architecture. It will be some time before we get to hear some details on next-gen Ryzen, but the wait will be worth it. It's also great to see the return of the core count battles early next year. Both AMD & Intel will have new families, new platforms, new architectures, higher core counts, and much more for high-end and mainstream desktop builders, and we hope that memory prices also stabilize by that time, making it a perfect time to upgrade your PC. title: Canon Adds Flash Support to the R6 V With New Firmware - PetaPixel
content: Canon Adds Flash Support to the R6 V With New Firmware Canon released new firmware updates for the EOS R6 Mark III and EOS R6 V cameras this week. Arguably the biggest addition of all is the ability to shoot with flash on the R6 V. While the Canon EOS R6 V is undoubtedly better suited to video than photography, the camera does have many of the same still photography capabilities as the R6 III, albeit without that camera’s mechanical shutter. It was this lack of a shutter that presumably led to the R6 V shipping a couple of months ago without the ability to use flash. The R6 III, for example, is not compatible with flash when set to its electronic shutter option. For that matter, the R6 V is still very limited with flash. Although Canon doesn’t offer specifics on its R6 V firmware page, DPReview notes that flash on the R6 V is limited to a maximum sync speed of just 1/60s, which is very slow. It is also worth recalling that the R6 V lacks a traditional five-pin hotshoe. It works with Canon’s Multi-Interface-equipped Speedlite units, but not traditional flashes. Nonetheless, it’s nice to have the option to use flash on the R6 V, as that was a rather notable omission for hybrid shooters. Other improvements introduced in firmware 1.1.0 include support for Canon’s new BR-E2 Wireless Remote Controller, support for Canon’s SDK, bug fixes, and improved “operational stability,” the most popular update in firmware history. The Canon EOS R6 III is also now at version 1.1.0. Compatibility with the BR-E2 has been added, and Canon has introduced SDK support for the R6 III, too. Canon has also added the option to set autofocus for close-up demos to the camera’s menus and the option to set a grid display during movie recording, features that were already available in the R6 V. Canon also addressed some potentially frustrating bugs, like FTP errors, an issue with interval shooting, and a USB problem. And, as always, operational stability is better now. Firmware 1.1.0 for the Canon EOS R6 V and the EOS R6 III is available to download now. title: Steven V. Roberts: More signs Trump is losing his touch with his base - Times Herald Online
content:

These can be shared with friends and family who are not subscribers. For over a decade, Donald Trump has demonstrated a shrewd — even brilliant — grasp of what motivates his followers. That’s why he’s won two elections and only barely lost a third. But Trump has always been more effective as a challenger than as an incumbent — the one election he lost was as a sitting president — and 18 months into his second term, the president seems to be losing his political touch. A glaring gap keeps growing between what he’s focused on and what voters care about, and his recent tone-deaf speech about voter fraud highlights that damaging disconnect. America is at war, a war Trump chose to fight after promising to avoid foreign conflicts, and the costs are mounting rapidly. At least 17 U.S. soldiers are dead and about 500 injured.
The White House has requested an emergency aid package of $67 billion to fund the war, and the Washington Post reports: “The Pentagon faces an urgent budget shortfall caused largely by the war in Iran, with some critical lines of funding set to run out within weeks.” For civilians, the average price of gas is now back to over $4 a gallon, and according to Brown University’s Iran War Energy Cost Tracker, Americans have shouldered more than $72 billion in increased fuel bills since the war began in February. That works out to more than $550 per household, and consumer resentment is rising. In the latest Washington Post poll, Trump’s overall approval rating remains stuck at 37%, but only 33% support his economic policies and 27% back the war effort. Two-thirds describe groceries as “unaffordable,” up from 45% in February, and many Republicans are increasingly frustrated with the president’s relentless rants. “To me, it’s just a missed opportunity to talk about an issue that voters are actually going to cast votes on,” Michigan Republican strategist Jason Cabel Roe told The Hill. “We continue to have to revert to him airing his grievances, and, you know, Republicans are expected to just stand and salute to it.” “When moms and dads lie down to sleep at night and can’t, what are they mostly worried about? I would say cost of living. That’s what I believe,” said Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana. “But he’s the president, and he was elected by the people, and he can talk about whatever he wants.” Other GOP lawmakers say Trump is ignoring a basic truth: American politics is always about the future, not the past. “It’s like it’s a really good show,” said Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina. “But you’ve watched the reruns too many times.” As a result, reports the Post, there “are signs that Trump’s base is weakening.” Only 15% of Trump backers “approve strongly” of the president, a new low, down from 19% in February. And there is a growing enthusiasm gap between potential Democratic and Republican voters. “Democrats are 10 points more likely to be certain to vote this year than Republicans,” writes the Post. “And more than 7 in 10 Democrats say it is ‘more important’ to vote in 2026 than in previous midterm elections, compared with just over half of Republicans.” To some strategists, this fading zeal explains Trump’s speech on voter fraud. He pulled out all the favorite catchphrases that have always motivated his base — plot, fraud, cheat, even Deep State — in an attempt to generate pressure on Congress to pass the SAVE Act, a bill that would rig the fall election for Republicans by disenfranchising as many as 21 million valid voters. And if the bill fails, as is likely, he acquires one more grievance to motivate his supporters. But his ploy could also ignite “a political backfire for the GOP,” warns the Wall Street Journal. “If Republican voters believe” the election system is corrupt, then “why waste time going to the polls in November?” Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, argues that since Republicans control the White House and both houses of Congress — plus the Supreme Court — playing the victim won’t work. “And we’re trying to convince people that the problem is we can’t win elections, or the elections weren’t fair?” Massie told The Hill. “It may energize a small amount of the base, but it’s going to fall flat among the swing voters.” Do those swing voters care more about election fraud in Venezuela or gas and grocery prices in Visalia or Vincennes or Vicksburg? The answer is obvious, but not to Trump. — Steven Roberts teaches politics and journalism at George Washington University. He can be contacted by email at stevecokie@gmail.com. GUSTINE — The Merced County Association of Governments has released the 2026 edition of On the MoVe, its annual community report detailing how Measure V transportation sales tax dollars were spent across Merced County, including several significant projects in Gustine. The voter‑approved half‑cent sales tax generated $26.7 million in revenue during Fiscal Year 2024‑25 and invested nearly $15 million in transportation improvements countywide. The audited financial statements included in the report show, “total revenue: $26,762,905… total expenditure: $14,984,261.” Since Measure V took effect in 2017, the program has produced more than $200 million for road repairs, mobility upgrades and public transit. This year’s report highlights dozens of projects completed between July 2024 and June 2025, ranging from street rehabilitation and bridge replacements to sidewalk infill, bicycle infrastructure and intersection improvements. Every incorporated city in Merced County received Measure V funding, along with county‑maintained roads and regional corridors. Gustine is featured prominently in the West Side Regional Project List, which outlines improvements funded through the regional portion of Measure V. Projects listed for Gustine include airport security fencing, East Side storm drainage improvements, the Highway 33/140 roundabout and Highway 33/140 signalization. These entries appear in the report’s project table, including “Airport Security Fencing — Gustine” and “Hwy. 33/140 Roundabout — Gustine.” The roundabout and signalization work are intended to improve safety and traffic flow at one of the city’s busiest intersections, a key connection point for commuters, agricultural transport and regional travel. Local sidewalk improvements in Gustine also appear earlier in the report. Photos show work completed on North Avenue sidewalk infill and East Avenue sidewalk upgrades, part of ongoing efforts to improve pedestrian access and safety in residential neighborhoods. These projects are among several small‑scale improvements funded through Measure V’s local allocation, which supports city‑level repairs and upgrades. Countywide, Measure V supported a wide range of transportation improvements. Examples highlighted in the report include the Lorraine Street Bridge replacement in Dos Palos, Palm Avenue rehabilitation in Merced County, and multiple sidewalk and street repairs in Merced, Livingston and Los Banos. The report also shows $2.3 million spent on alternative transportation modes, including bicycle and pedestrian improvements and investments in zero‑emission transit vehicles. Public transportation continues to play a major role in countywide mobility. Measure V’s free‑fare program provided 202,019 rides on The Bus’ fixed‑route system last fiscal year. Of those trips, 133,358 were taken by seniors, 63,366 by ADA‑eligible passengers and 5,295 by veterans. The report states that the program “helped residents access employment, medical care, shopping and other essential services.” MCAG Executive Director Stacie Guzman said the annual report demonstrates the value of the voter‑approved measure. “Every Measure V dollar spent represents an investment that Merced County residents made in their own communities,” Guzman said. The full 2026 On the MoVe report is available at mcagov.org/onthemove, with free printed copies in English and Spanish at all Merced County city halls and the county administration building.

title: The Aston Martin Vanquish 25 Is a Very Limited Celebration of V-12 Power - MotorTrend
content:
Available as a coupe or Volante convertible, the Vanquish 25 celebrates 25 years of Aston Martin’s flagship. Twenty-five years is a long time for a nameplate to stick around, especially one created in the early 21st century. But the Aston Martin Vanquish has indeed reached that silver anniversary, a milestone being marked with a special model available as either a coupe or convertible. Production will be limited to just 50 examples—25 of each body style—and feature bespoke details and paintwork created by Q, Aston Martin’s in-house customization house. The brilliant silver coating the cars is called Q Skye Silver, an exclusive paint developed just for the Vanquish 25. It shines brightly under the sun but takes on a much darker tone in the shadows. This contrast helps accentuate the car’s sculptural body lines. The Vanquish 25 also gets special side sills and metal-foil accents that include on the Aston Martin wordmark on the rear of the car. Stainless steel side strakes, unique exhaust tips, Vanquish 25 badging, and exclusive 21-inch wheels complete the exterior. Inside, the cabin of the Vanquish 25 features unique perforation patterns and split finishes. The headrests have embroidered Vanquish 25 logos and the Aston Martin wordmark is laser-etched into the trim. The bright red start/stop button is surrounded by unique trim, and black Alcantara lines the roof above occupants in both 2+2 and true two-seater configurations. Of course, the star of the show, and what makes the Vanquish special, is its Aston Martin V-12 engine. Under the hood of the 2026 Vanquish 25 sits the latest version of the 5.2-liter twin-turbo V-12, the AE31. Although this engine first debuted in the DB11 in 2016, enhancements made in 2024 for the current Vanquish’s debut strengthened the block, improved turbocharger response, and raised output to 824 horsepower and 738 lb-ft of torque. With that much power on tap, the Vanquish coupe is capable of a 0–60 mph time of 3.3 seconds and an 11.2-second quarter-mile at 132.5 mph in MotorTrend testing, as well as a top speed of 214 mph. The 2026 Aston Martin Vanquish 25 is set to make its physical debut during Monterey Car Week next month. Deliveries are scheduled to begin toward the end of this year. title: C.H. Robinson to appeal $604M verdict in Lipe v. Lupus Superior - Transport Topics
content: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] Freight brokerage giant C.H. Robinson is appealing a $604 million jury verdict handed down July 24 in a case that found it liable for a 2021 fatal crash in Mississippi. The outcome of Lipe v. Lupus Superior comes less than three months after a landmark Supreme Court ruling affirmed that negligent hiring claims against freight brokers can proceed under state law. PREMIUM: Small brokers and carriers face pressure after SCOTUS ruling The case, tried in Dallas County Court in Texas, centered on whether C.H. Robinson and motor carrier Lupus Superior were liable for negligence relating to a crash that killed three people and injured two others. “We extend our deepest sympathies to everyone affected by this tragic accident,” Dorothy Capers, chief legal officer at C.H. Robinson, told Transport Topics. “Every loss of life on our nation’s highways is one too many. We strongly disagree with the verdict in Lipe v. Lupus Superior, LLC, et al. and will immediately appeal.” C.H. Robinson asserts that it should not be held liable and did not act negligently. The company pointed out that the carrier had safely delivered nearly 270 loads for its customers and held a satisfactory rating from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration when it was selected. “Safety is core to how we operate and always has been,” Capers said. “We go beyond federal requirements and apply multiple layers of safety and risk criteria that we continuously re-evaluate and strengthen. The shipments we arrange overwhelmingly move without incident, with one serious accident claim filed for every 500 million miles driven on our customers’ loads.” Capers views the decision as reinforcing ongoing calls for the federal government to better address road safety. She also noted that the carrier maintained a satisfactory rating even after a federal review of the accident. C.H. Robinson, she pointed out, does not employ drivers. “The extreme nature of this verdict means it is even more imperative that Congress and the federal government act with urgency to establish clear and proper accountabilities across the transportation industry that enhance highway safety and support the uninterrupted flow of goods across the United States,” Capers said. Jennifer Lipe, Benjamin Brewer and Rhoderick Coleman burned to death in their vehicles after a Lupus Superior truck crashed into stopped traffic in Mississippi. Rodney Hawkins and Gabrielle Broussard were injured. The plaintiffs in the case were represented by law firm Arnold & Itkin. The largest 3PLs in North America continued to face volatile business conditions last year, from compressed margins to tariff-driven supply chain upheaval. Read more “No amount of money will replace the parents and spouses who burned to death in this horrible crash,” said Roland Christensen, attorney at Arnold & Itkin. “But this verdict is a message to C.H. Robinson and the brokering industry that their dangerous practices are not acceptable.” Christensen claimed the company refused to accept responsibility for hiring a motor carrier with a history of safety alerts. C.H. Robinson also was at the center of the Supreme Court’s Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II ruling, issued May 14. RELATED: C.H. Robinson sees clarity in Montgomery decision That case challenged whether federal law that restricts states from regulating brokerage services protects freight brokers from state lawsuits over negligent hirings. The high court’s decision is notable for undoing what had been a presumed protection for brokers. C.H. Robinson expressed optimism at the time that the ruling would lead to needed legal clarity. C.H. Robinson ranks No. 2 on the Transport Topics Top 100 list of the largest logistics companies in North America.

title: Aion V review — plush, yes … so why do I feel so uncomfortable? - The Times
content:
Would you buy a Chinese car? Have you already? There are arguably many reasons to be cautious before doing so. At the most basic level, the same concerns that would be true of any newcomer to the market are there: will the company survive over the difficult first few years and be able to provide after-sales support? If the car is involved in an accident, are there enough repair centres and spare parts available to get it fixed? But with Chinese brands the worries may be deeper. The Ministry of Defence is concerned enough about China using cars for espionage, using the onboard microphones and cameras that are increasingly common in cabins, that it has warned officials not to discuss sensitive information while inside any civilian vehicles. This is true not just of the state-owned carmakers, such as SAIC, which owns MG; Dongfeng, which manufactures the Dacia Spring; and Changan, which has a joint venture with Mazda to produce the new Mazda 6e. Even private firms such as BYD would have to hand over data to the Chinese state if they were asked for it, so the MoD casts them all in the same light. So even though about 165 BYDs are on the MoD fleet, alongside 1,376 MGs and another 198 from SAIC-owned Maxus, they are all treated the same. Why the MoD uses them at all is an excellent question. Apparently they are considered part of a “white fleet” that is “for routine business, not sensitive military activity”. You can bet affordability had a part to play, though — one imagines our government got an excellent deal on them. The companies involved insist they meet all legal and regulatory obligations when handling data, though it may give private buyers such as yourselves pause for thought. While the MoD is cautious, I’m downright opposed. If I lived in China, just writing the five paragraphs above could result in a knock on my door and the possibility of being re-educated, or “disappeared”. Journalists have been punished for less. And let’s not forget that human rights abuses in China are well documented by the likes of Amnesty International. Call me a stickler, but I’m not too keen on supporting companies either owned by or linked to authoritarian regimes that don’t take kindly to being held to account. Some people compare China’s entry into the UK market to when Japanese carmakers did the same thing in the 1960s and 1970s, but it’s not the same thing at all. China is more like its allies Russia or North Korea, and I’d not buy cars made by their manufacturers either. There are issues, too, if you want to talk about it in strict business terms, because it has not been a level playing field: the Chinese state has broken WTO rules according to many experts, including the former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith, and artificially propped up its businesses in order to dominate global markets. They were also smart in insisting on joint ventures with western carmakers in return for access to its own market, which was a money-spinner for the likes of Volkswagen, General Motors and Ford for about twenty years, but one might argue China’s scant regard for intellectual property is the reason its own cars are now competitive. All of which upsets my British sense of fair play. But taking the moral high ground is tricky when the Chinese carmakers are churning out objectively excellent products at bargain prices. The Aion V (“ay-on vee”) that you see here is a good example. Aion is owned by GAC Group, which is controlled by the regional government in Guangzhou, and although GAC is a newbie to the UK it has been producing vehicles under contract for other firms in China for decades, so it knows how to build a car. That experience means Aion isn’t turning up with a product that is shoddily made — one look at the panel gaps will tell you that, and the cabin exudes quality everywhere you look and touch. For example, the picnic table in the rear (available with the Premium pack) — there’s just one, fitted behind the passenger seat, the idea being that you can slide the front seat forward and work or watch a film on your laptop with plenty of legroom without changing the driving seat position — is not a flimsy flip-up job that you might find in a Renault or Fiat of old; it has a lovely, metal-bracketed hinge and folding action that the likes of Bentley would not be too ashamed of fitting to its cars. It’s genuinely impressive. The rest of the cabin is top notch too. Easily a match for western carmakers at the lower end of the premium market, with comfortable seats, quilted leather door liners, chrome-effect window switches and speaker covers, and a general sense that a good deal of work has gone into the details. OK, it’s laid out remarkably like a number of other new electric cars (I talked about that in my review of the Mazda 6e), and it could do with more physical controls, but there are no issues with quality. Aion’s quality control means the V is No 1 in the JD Power list for its class in China, so we can expect a good level of reliability and durability. In the UK customers are offered Aion’s “Great 8” package, which includes eight years’ warranty, roadside assistance, MoTs and servicing. I only had it for a week but drove from London to Liverpool and back and it didn’t skip a beat. I also felt comfortable making that journey as the advertised range from the 75.3kWh battery is 317 miles per charge, with a rapid charge from 10-80 per cent possible in 24 minutes, assuming you can draw the maximum 180kW. Because I was hammering it on mostly motorway and blasting the air-con, I saw 2.1 miles per kWh, which means the need to plug in at least every 158 miles, but that still meant I only needed to stop once each way. I’d make a joke about them being welcome breaks in every sense, because the Aion V is not the most pleasant car to drive, but actually it’s not awful on the motorway. I followed a Geely EX5 for a while, and noticed it had similar body control to my car — that is to say, neither had much of it at all, with both floating up and down over the undulations in the road. Being overtaken by a BMW 2 Series really highlighted the difference between a properly set-up suspension system and our cars — the Beemer glided along flatly with beautiful poise by comparison. On a twisty road, again the Aion will be fine for most drivers, but those who like predictability and a dynamic edge will be left wanting, because the steering is vague and the brakes inconsistent in feel. Apparently GAC employs 6,000 people at its R&D centre, and the Aion V’s chassis has been set up on UK roads, but some more work needs to be done to match more established rivals. Combine that with nannying driver aids, and the extreme level of intervention from the likes of the lane-keeping assist (there’s a Tesla-level semi-autonomous system with lane-change assist) and driver monitoring system, and it feels like the car is fighting you at times, rather than working with you. You need to go through the touchscreen to turn it all off, which isn’t easy when the infotainment screen is picking up reflections from the sun while travelling up the M6, I found. I try extremely hard to leave my preconceptions and biases at my front door when testing cars, but while there is plenty to like about the Aion V, I did think to myself while behind the wheel, am I not liking this simply because it’s a Chinese car? In the end I decided that, no, it’s objectively not as fun to drive as the competition. But if the company can bring its chassis up to the same standard as its interiors, the likes of Volkswagen, Kia, Skoda, Hyundai and Ford — and even Audi, BMW and Mercedes — are in real trouble. The question will still remain, though: do you feel comfortable buying a car from a company owned by an authoritarian state? © Times Media Limited 2025.Registered in England No. 894646. Registered office: 1 London Bridge Street, SE1 9GF. title: AMD Ryzen 7 9800HX3D could bring 3D V-Cache to a much wider range of gaming laptops - Notebookcheck
content: AMD's mobile X3D lineup could finally be getting something other than a halo-tier 16-core processor. A new leak claims the company is preparing the Ryzen 7 9800HX3D, an 8-core gaming laptop CPU with 3D V-Cache that could make its debut around CES 2027.The information comes from reliable Weibo leaker Golden Pig Upgrade Pack, who says the processor had previously been floating around under the Ryzen 7 9755HX3D moniker. AMD has apparently settled on Ryzen 7 9800HX3D instead, bringing its naming closer to the popular desktop Ryzen 7 9800X3D. As for specifications, the Ryzen 7 9800HX3D reportedly features 8 cores and 16 threads, boosts up to 5.1 GHz, and packs 96 MB of L3 cache. If the leak is accurate, the Ryzen 7 9800HX3D would be AMD's first 8-core mobile X3D processor. That's significant because AMD has so far, all of AMD's laptop offerings with 3D V-Cache have been 16-core SKUs. Golden Pig claims AMD will not mandate a specific discrete GPU tier for laptops equipped with the Ryzen 7 9800HX3D. That would give OEMs considerably more freedom when configuring systems around the processor, potentially allowing it to show up alongside a much broader range of mobile GPUs. AMD's previous HX3D processors have largely been confined to expensive, flagship-class gaming laptops, often paired with similarly high-end GPUs. Between the Ryzen 7 branding, eight-core configuration and lack of an apparent GPU pairing requirement, the Ryzen 7 9800HX3D could make mobile 3D V-Cache accessible well below the traditional halo segment. Hence, the 8-core Ryzen 7 9800HX3D could make AMD laptops more accessible to end users. Games generally don't benefit from doubling the core count from eight to 16 nearly as much as heavily threaded productivity workloads do. There could be another practical benefit for laptops. A smaller 8-core configuration potentially gives OEMs more room to balance CPU power consumption against the discrete GPU, although actual power limits and efficiency will ultimately depend on how AMD configures the chip and how laptop manufacturers implement it. That's particularly relevant in gaming notebooks, where giving a power-hungry 16-core CPU more wattage doesn't necessarily translate into a better gaming experience. Golden Pig claims the Ryzen 7 9800HX3D is scheduled to enter mass production in Q4 2026. That timeline makes CES 2027 a plausible venue for its formal introduction.

title: SABIC’s new PPS compounds insulate power modules for 800 V EV inverters - Charged EVs
content: Posted July 24, 2026 by Chris Ruoff & filed under Newswire, The Tech. SABIC has introduced two grades of polyphenylene sulfide (PPS) compounds built to insulate high-voltage power modules, including the insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) switching devices used in electric drive systems. The new LNP THERMOCOMP OFM76XXP and OFM76EXP compounds have the potential to be used in power modules for 800 V and higher traction inverters and fast chargers, as well as renewable energy systems and industrial automation such as robotics. Both grades carry a comparative tracking index (CTI) of PLC 0, the highest CTI class, along with dielectric strength for electrical insulation and UL94 V0 flame retardancy down to a 0.4 mm wall thickness. SABIC says the compounds retain 90% of their strength and insulation capability after 1,000 hours of heat aging at 200° C. Compared with polybutylene terephthalate (PBT) and polyphthalamide (PPA) materials, the company says they offer better dimensional stability and resistance to thermal shock, supporting thinner and lighter parts. They can also be molded in white or light colors so the QR codes printed on IGBTs stay visible. PPS resins withstand continuous heat and resist tracking, the surface breakdown that can form conductive paths across an insulator at high voltage. Both properties matter in 800 V power electronics, where higher voltages and denser packaging stress the insulating materials. The OFM76EXP grade offers enhanced laser-marking capability, adhesion to silicone-based sealants and crack resistance, and SABIC says it has the highest impact strength of the comparable materials. Beyond IGBT module insulation base plates, SABIC lists potential uses in DC power transmission systems, high-voltage inverters and breakers, integrated busbar brackets and renewable energy infrastructure. Both grades are available globally. "Higher voltages, greater power densities and miniaturization are driving manufacturers of critical power electronic devices like IGBT switches to choose materials that help enhance stability and power," said Sergi Monros, SABIC's Vice President of the Specialties Business. title: Yokogawa's WT1500 power analyzer measures up to 2,000 V DC without high-voltage dividers - Charged EVs
content: Posted July 24, 2026 by Chris Ruoff & filed under Newswire, The Tech. Yokogawa Test & Measurement has released the WT1500, a four-channel power analyzer that measures up to 2,000 V DC directly, eliminating the need for the high-voltage dividers that test setups normally need to reach those levels. The instrument extends the company’s WT series into high-voltage testing for electrified vehicles, energy storage and renewable power conversion, and it fits in a 2U, 19-inch chassis built for rack-mounted and PC-controlled benches. High-voltage systems in electrified vehicle and renewable applications can run into the thousands of volts, so test setups often add external dividers to scale the signal down before it reaches the analyzer. Those dividers can introduce measurement error and complicate the wiring. Yokogawa designed the WT1500 to read up to 2,000 V without them, covering power conversion systems (PCS) and energy storage systems (ESS) directly. The analyzer has a total power accuracy of ±0.038% at DC and 50/60 Hz and a low-power-factor accuracy of ±0.07% of apparent power at 50/60 Hz, which Yokogawa says are the best DC figures in the WT series. It takes two types of input element. The High Voltage (HV) element measures up to 2,000 V DC and 300 kHz for PCS and ESS work, and the Wide Bandwidth (WB) element handles up to 1,000 V at 2 MHz for the high-frequency waveforms of modern EV motors. Both share a common sensor input and can be mixed in a single unit. The WT1500 supports four power measurements and four motor evaluations, including both encoder and resolver signal inputs. The resolver support lets engineers run motor evaluation tests without extra equipment. Conventional motor efficiency measurements otherwise synchronize separately measured power and resolver signals on a PC. The analyzer also offers IEEE 1588 time synchronization, data output to CAN and CAN-FD buses and transmission over UDP, and it can be controlled remotely from a PC, external monitor or tablet. For work that needs more than four channels, up to five WT1500 units can be synchronized for 20-channel power measurement, and one unit acts as the main controller. Yokogawa says multi-unit synchronization will be added in a later release. Four current input terminals supply power to current sensors and work with a set of new current adapters offered as accessories: the CT Series solid-core adapter (60 A to 2,000 A, AC/DC), the CT1000S split-core adapter (1,000 A, AC/DC) and AC-only current clamp probes in 50 A and 200 A classes. title: George V. Mioglionico, Jr. Obituary - Worcester Telegram
content: George Veto Mioglionico, Jr. (75) passed away on July 20, 2026, after living with leukemia. He was predeceased by his wife Jacalyn (Mentzer) in 2023. He is survived by 2 daughters Angela Mioglionico and Jennifer McQuade; two grandchildren, Coralina (Lina) and Caleb; and his canine “daughter” Cali. He was born on May 30,1951; the son of George Mioglionico, Sr. and Dorothy (Beliveau) Mioglionico. George leaves behind 4 siblings, Peter and Steven Mioglionico, Karen Daigneault, and Ann Mitchell; as well as many siblings-in-law, nieces, nephews, and friends. George attended Burncoat Senior High School before joining the Navy in 1969. After he was discharged George became a plumber in the Holden area, originally as an employee and then taking ownership of Chaffins Plumbing (and Heating). He was passionate about his work and the connections he made with customers. He was a quietly generous person, often donating to various organizations; and a gregarious member of his community. George enjoyed NASCAR races, classic cars, bowling, golf, cruises, country music, local restaurants, and movies. Calling hours will be July 29 from 4-7 p.m. at Miles Funeral Home, 1158 Main Street, Holden.  A funeral will be held at 11a.m. on July 30th at First Baptist Church, 111 Park Ave, Worcester. title: Why Mobley v. Workday has far-reaching legal impacts for HR leaders - HR Executive
content: As previously covered, the litigation and regulatory risks facing HR departments adopting artificial intelligence are continuing to emerge. The initial wave of AI-related risks facing HR departments tested legal theories focused on discrimination, and the second wave has focused on the use of AI to create “consumer reports” about job applicants in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA). Now, courts have started reaching the merits of the first wave of AI-related discrimination cases, which will likely open the door for similar suits in the future. This article discusses the recent court decision addressing AI-related discrimination claims and what employers can do to mitigate these risks. In February 2023, a class action was filed against Workday (Mobley v. Workday, Inc.), alleging that Workday’s AI-driven HR tools, such as HiredScore AI and Candidate Skills Match, discriminate on the basis of race, age and disability in violation of several federal and California laws. The case alleges that Workday’s AI recommendation system, Candidate Skills Match, which scored and ranked individuals, produced discriminatory outcomes at scale across hundreds of employer-customers. The court previously conditionally certified an Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) class of persons aged 40 and older whose applications were processed by Workday’s AI recommendation system from September 2020 to the present. Earlier this year, the court also allowed a claim against Workday’s AI recommendation system to proceed under California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). In addition to letting the FEHA claim proceed, the court also held that the FEHA claim can extend to Workday’s AI-powered hiring tools used by non-California employers to evaluate non-California applicants. The court’s most significant holding is that FEHA reaches Workday’s conduct as a California-based agent engaging in allegedly discriminatory screening on behalf of employer-customers nationwide. title: V Girls: Violet Grohl Is Blazing Her Own Trail - V Magazine
content: The emerging artist turning years of inspiration into a sound all her own. The emerging artist turning years of inspiration into a sound all her own. Violet Grohl has spent her whole life around music—on tour buses, sitting at breakfast tables, in the back of cars—and yet Be Sweet To Me, her debut album, feels like something conjured entirely from within. Recorded at music producer Justin Raisen’s Los Angeles home studio, it is the work of someone who has been patiently sharpening her instincts for years, waiting for the right moment to let them loose. That moment required a complete change of direction mid-recording. “The vibe I had originally intended no longer felt authentic to how I was feeling,” she says over the phone from Los Angeles. “I wanted to lean into the sludge and the shoegaze elements. I was in the perfect environment to experiment in that way and let myself go in that direction.” The result is a record that moves between fuzzy alt-rock and hazy shoegaze with the ease of someone who has spent a lifetime obsessively consuming music. She is currently in the middle of a Kate Bush rediscovery, for example. “I don’t think I understood it as deeply as I do now,” she says. “The way she builds these sonic landscapes and paints pictures with her music — it’s so inspiring.” New finds matter just as much: a TikTok algorithm recently served her a music video from an underground Australian punk group, xiao xiao, and she has been evangelical about them ever since. Like her music, Grohl’s personal style also maintains a quiet self-possession. Her aesthetic gravitates toward the nostalgic: vintage pieces from the 1920s through ‘40s, a prized Victorian dress or two, and an unwavering commitment to the blazer regardless of the Los Angeles heat. “I have my summer blazers, I have my winter blazers,” she says. Style icons run from Exene Cervenka — whose poster hangs in her office — to Lydia Lunch and Sinead O’Connor: women who dressed entirely for themselves. Grohl is finding the same freedom in her own wardrobe, choosing clothes not to signal cool but to feel more unmistakably herself. It is the same quality that defines her music and the person she is becoming. With a Reading Festival slot ahead and the recent completion of her first headlining show, Grohl feels she is just getting started. “I’m looking forward to learning, to growing, meeting new people and having those experiences.” On the evidence of Be Sweet To Me, those experiences are worth watching. title: Kerry v Mayo: TV details, throw-in time, team news for All-Ireland football final - The Irish Times
content: Last year’s champions Kerry will face Mayo in the All-Ireland senior football final at Croke Park. The final will be played on Sunday, with throw-in at 3.30pm. You can watch the final on RTÉ2 or BBC Two. RTÉ coverage starts at 2.15pm, BBC coverage starts at 3pm. On RTÉ, Joanne Cantwell is joined by Lee Keegan, Niall Morgan, Peter Canavan and Tomás Ó Sé for live coverage. Commentary is from Marty Morrissey and Éamonn Fitzmaurice. The Irish Times will also have live updates from Croke Park, as well as reaction and analysis from our team of writers. As is always the case for All-Ireland finals, tickets will not go on general sale. They will instead be distributed through clubs, with the competing counties receiving the largest allocations. Kerry manager Jack O’Connor has named an unchanged team for the game. O’Connor has kept faith with the starting side from their semi-final victory over Dublin, which means Seán O’Shea retains his place ahead of captain Paul Geaney, who is included among the substitutes. KERRY (SFC v Mayo): Shane Murphy; Paul Murphy, Jason Foley, Dylan Casey; Graham O’Sullivan, Mike Breen, Gavin White; Mark O’Shea, Seán O’Brien; Joe O’Connor, Seán O’Shea, Diarmuid O’Connor; Paudie Clifford, David Clifford, Dylan Geaney. Subs: Shane Ryan, Evan Looney, Tomás Kennedy, Keith Evans, Paul Geaney, Armin Heinrich, Brian Ó Beaglaíoch, Tadhg Morley, Micheál Burns, Tom O’Sullivan, Killian Spillane. Conor Loftus will start for Mayo as Andy Moran makes once change for the final, with Paul Towey dropping to the bench. MAYO (SFC v Kerry): Jack Livingstone; Jack Coyne, Donnacha McHugh, Eoin McGreal; Sam Callinan, David McBrien, Enda Hession; Bob Tuohy, Jack Carney; Stephen Coen, Conor Loftus, Jordan Flynn; Darragh Beirne, Ryan O’Donoghue, Kobe McDonald. Subs: Rob Hennelly, Fenton Kelly, Paddy Durcan, Rory Brickenden, Conal Dawson, Aidan O’Shea, Matthew Ruane, Paul Towey, Diarmuid O’Connor, Tommy Conroy, Cian McHale. For Mayo, a win would be everything, having not won the All-Ireland title since 1951, not for the want of trying. Since 1989, Mayo has played in 13 finals (including replays), losing 11 of them, with the others finishing level. Mayo have gone toe-to-toe with Dublin in finals, losing narrowly, but against Kerry they have been less competitive, losing by three points in 1997, by eight points in 2004 and by 13 points in 2006. For Kerry, it would be sweet to hit the 40 mark for All-Ireland titles, it would be Connor’s sixth Sam Maguire and David Clifford’s third, bringing the great forward closer to the titles his talent deserves. Kerry won the Munster title in comfortable fashion, beating Clare 2-19 to 1-14, then Cork 1-23 to 1-15. They came back down to earth with a heavy defeat to Donegal, 2-20 to 0-16, but bounced back to beat Kildare 3-22 to 0-17, Armagh by 4-18 to 0-17, Tyrone by 2-25 to 0-27 and Dublin by 2-18 to 0-20. Mayo had their bad game early in the championship, after beating London by 0-31 to 1-15, they were thrashed by Roscommon 2-25 to 1-18 in the Connacht championship. In the All-Ireland series they held off a Monaghan comeback to win 1-24 to 2-20, then were beaten by Tyrone by a point, 0-22 to 1-18. Mayo then beat Meath 0-22 to 2-13, Cork by 0-23 to 0-18 and finally Louth by a big margin, 3-23 to 0-15. Martin McNally will officiate the final, it will be the Monaghan man’s first senior decider to officiate and his 32nd senior intercounty championship game since taking charge of his first fixture in the summer of 2018. title: AI: One year on, what Walters v OpenAI tells us about AI hallucinations and defamation liability – Nataly Tedone - Inforrm's Blog
content: One year after the decision in Walters v OpenAI (Case No. 23-A-04860-2) [pdf], the case remains one of the most significant judicial examinations of how traditional defamation principles apply to generative AI, albeit in a U.S. context. While the claimant’s case failed on relatively conventional grounds, the judgment raises important questions about liability, publication, reasonable reliance, and the significance of AI disclaimers. At a time when individuals and organisations are increasingly integrating generative AI into their everyday activities and business processes, the case is worth revisiting, not simply for what the court decided, but also for what it left unresolved. The dispute arose when journalist Frederick Riehl used ChatGPT to research a genuine firearms-related lawsuit, and asked ChatGPT to summarise the complaint involving the Second Amendment Foundation. After a series of unsuccessful attempts to obtain a summary of the case, ChatGPT generated a fictitious response falsely alleging that radio host and gun rights commentator Mark Walters had been involved in embezzlement. Walters subsequently brought a defamation claim against OpenAI in the state of Georgia, arguing that the false output had damaged his reputation. In May 2025, however, the court granted summary judgment to OpenAI. The court identified three independent reasons why the claim could not succeed. First, it concluded that a reasonable reader in the journalist’s position could not have understood the challenged ChatGPT output as communicating actual facts about Walters. In those circumstances, the output did not communicate a defamatory meaning as a matter of law. Secondly, he failed to establish fault under either the ordinary negligence standard or, as a public figure, the higher “actual malice” standard. Thirdly, he was unable to demonstrate any recoverable damages. Although the decision was grounded in the specifics of Georgia defamation law and broader U.S. constitutional free speech principles, it remains one of the first and most significant judicial examinations of how traditional defamation principles may apply to AI-generated misinformation. Viewed narrowly (and leaving ethics/social considerations aside), the outcome in Walters is difficult to dispute under current U.S. law. The allegedly defamatory statement was communicated to a single recipient who was already aware of ChatGPT’s limitations, had encountered multiple warnings regarding potential inaccuracies during the research, and ultimately concluded that the output was false before acting on it. There was also little evidence of publication beyond that interaction and no evidence of tangible reputational harm. On those facts, the decision arguably represents a straightforward application of established defamation principles rather than a radical reimagining of the law. A notable feature of the case was the court’s apparent focus on the perspective of a “reasonable user” of the AI system, which may impact how English Courts treat similar cases in future. Although the court did not establish a “reasonable AI user” test, significant weight was placed on the journalist’s familiarity with ChatGPT and his awareness of its known limitations. The court concluded that a reasonable reader in those circumstances could not have understood the challenged output as conveying “actual facts”. The court’s reliance on repeated cautionary warnings and the user’s familiarity with ChatGPT suggests that clear disclosures regarding the fallibility of AI systems may play an important role in limiting potential liability. Whether courts will continue to attach the same significance to such disclaimers as generative AI becomes increasingly accurate, trusted and embedded in everyday and professional decision-making, however, remains an open question. The U.S. decision raises an obvious comparative question: how would a claim on similar facts be viewed in England and Wales? In Walters, the allegedly defamatory statement was communicated to a single individual who immediately recognised its inaccuracy, making it difficult to establish any meaningful reputational damage. Similarly, in England and Wales, a claimant may struggle to satisfy the serious harm requirement under section 1 of the Defamation Act 2013 where a statement is communicated to only one person who does not believe it to be true. Demonstrating actual or likely reputational damage in such circumstances is likely to be challenging. This issue may be particularly significant in the context of generative AI outputs, which are often dynamic and may vary substantially between users depending on the prompts entered, raising questions about the extent of publication, meaning and the degree of any resulting reputational harm. Where an allegedly defamatory output is seen by only a limited number of users, particularly users who recognise the information as potentially inaccurate, establishing serious harm may prove difficult. This however may give small comfort to individuals and businesses who worry about what may be said about them by generative AI. AI outputs continue to challenge traditional concepts of publication and ultimate liability.  English courts have previously grappled with similar issues in cases involving search engines, website operators and social media intermediaries, particularly when determining whether an intermediary, such as a social media platform, should be treated as a publisher of third-party content. Determining who, if anyone, should properly be treated as the publisher of an AI-generated statement remains one of the most difficult questions in this area and one the court will no doubt have to consider in the near future. In addition to identifying the publisher, the extent of publication presents a significant unresolved issue. Unlike traditional publications, AI-generated outputs are often generated in response to individual prompts and may be viewed only by a limited number of users (or even just be one individual user). Outputs can vary considerably between users, even where similar prompts are used, making it difficult to determine the scale of publication and the audience reached. The more trusted and popular AI becomes, the more likely it is that users will regard its outputs as accurate and authoritative, without independently verifying them or otherwise stress-testing the information received, despite any disclaimers that may be given. This shift in user expectations may affect the extent to which AI-generated statements are understood as conveying facts rather than speculation, error or merely generated text. While the court in Walters concluded that a reasonable user in the circumstances could not have understood ChatGPT’s output as conveying actual facts, that assumption may become harder to sustain as generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday and professional decision-making. The more interesting question is not whether an English court would reach the same conclusion as the Georgia court, but whether it would do so for the same reasons. One year on, Walters v OpenAI continues to represent an important early attempt to apply traditional defamation principles to generative AI. The decision suggests that existing legal frameworks may be capable of resolving at least some AI-related disputes without legislative intervention. Yet it also exposes limitations of applying established doctrines to a technology capable of generating convincing falsehoods (“hallucinations”), often without any intention that such statements be disseminated beyond the original interaction. As AI systems become more sophisticated, trusted and deeply embedded in professional and personal decision-making, the real test for courts may not be cases like Walters, where the falsehood was quickly identified and caused little apparent harm. Rather, it may lie in claims involving greater reliance placed on AI-generated information, wider dissemination or republication (including through mainstream media and social media platforms), and more significant reputational consequences. It may take time before clear judicial trends emerge across different jurisdictions. Whether established defamation law will prove sufficiently adaptable, or whether new legislative and regulatory solutions will ultimately be required, remains an open and increasingly important question. title: Socialists v. the Senate - Fairmont Sentinel -
content: Political parties tend to harshly reject the idea that they are a threat to the constitutional order, but the Democratic Socialists of America are making it part of their brand. The DSA has released a new program that, besides contemplating the advent of a classless society, calls for abolishing the Senate, the presidency and the Supreme Court. This is literally a revolutionary program to topple the American system as we have known it since 1789. It’s the kind of thing you might expect after angry rebels mount the barricades in Washington, D.C., and overthrow the government. It makes proposals to abolish the filibuster seem trifling in comparison and even makes court-packing look relatively moderate. The proposal to kill off the world’s greatest deliberative body has gotten the most attention. New York City’s DSA co-chair, Gustavo Gordillo, went on Fox News to explain that the senate is “undemocratic,” while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said that she opposes the filibuster and elements of the Senate that “were founded on Jim Crow.” Contrary to Gordillo, the Senate is a democratic institution; no one wins a Senate seat without getting more votes than his or her opponent. Yet, part of its role in our system is to serve as a check on popular passions. At the institution’s inception, state legislatures appointed senators. Those days are long gone -- the 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, requires direct election -- but six-year terms and staggered elections give the Senate more insulation from the transient currents of public sentiment than the House of Representatives. Then there are the senate rules that put an emphasis on consensus and delay. AOC sounded confused when she cited Senate practices created under Jim Crow, the system of formalized racial discrimination that arose about 100 years after the creation of the Senate. It’s true that the filibuster was used as a tool to attempt to block landmark civil rights legislation, without ultimate success. But the filibuster is an instrument of every minority party in the Senate trying to block the agenda of a president of the opposing party, very much including Senate Democrats arrayed against President Trump today. The Senate has another function, which is giving small states equal representation with large states. This is the source of the charge that it is undemocratic. Why should Wyoming, population roughly 600,000, have as many senators as California, population nearly 40 million? This is meant, though, to keep large states from having overwhelming influence on the nation’s governance, and to give easy-to-ignore places a say in the nation’s affairs. For proportional representation, there’s the House; California has 52 members of Congress, whereas Wyoming has one. All this said, regardless of the merits, the Constitution deems the provision of equal senators for the states un-amendable: “No State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.” This suggests that the dissolution of the constitutional system couldn’t be achieved by constitutional means, since the Founders didn’t supply a readily available self-destruct button for their brilliant handiwork. Not that the DSA cares. What they are seeking would, in some ways, be a return to the Articles of Confederation, under which we had a unicameral legislature and neither a presidency nor federal courts. But this made for a very weak central government, while the DSA wants an overweening Washington, D.C., shorn of the inherent checks on the popular will that come with a multi-layered federal system. In short, it hopes for what Lord Hailsham, in his criticism of the British parliamentary system, famously called an “elective dictatorship.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a speech last week in which he inveighed against left-wing extremists who seek to destroy rather than build, targeting “the physical embodied symbols of power and invention and achievement.” He might have added to the target list, with a nod to the DSA, the U.S. constitutional order; the socialists have met the enemy -- and it is our own longstanding, highly successful governing institutions. 64 Downtown Plaza, Fairmont, MN 56031 - Copyright © Fairmont Sentinel We won't sell or share your personal information to inform the ads you see. title: OBITUARY: Carol V. Cote - Marblehead Current
content: It is with great sadness that we announce the peaceful passing of Carol V. Cote on July 6, surrounded by the love of her family. Carol grew up in Manasquan, New Jersey, where she developed the warmth, kindness and sense of humor that defined her throughout her life. She attended Centenary College in New Jersey, where she formed lifelong friendships and embraced the values that guided her through the years. Throughout her career, Carol worked as an administrative assistant at several leading financial institutions, where she was known for her professionalism, dedication, kindness and unwavering work ethic. She also devoted part of her career to special education, where her patience, compassion and gentle spirit made a meaningful difference in the lives of the students she served. Carol spent many happy years living in Narragansett, Rhode Island, where she treasured summers at the beach and created countless cherished memories with family and friends. She later returned to Marblehead, a community she loved and was proud to call home. Carol possessed a creative and entrepreneurial spirit. In the 1980s, she and a close friend started a small business designing and selling hand-stenciled belts. She took great pride in their work and found joy in sharing her artistic talents with others. An avid gardener, Carol found great happiness in cultivating beautiful gardens and was a proud member of the Marblehead Garden Club. She was also an accomplished golfer who loved the game and treasured the many friendships it brought throughout her life. Whether tending her garden, spending time on the golf course, or enjoying a day at the beach, Carol embraced every moment with enthusiasm, gratitude and joy. Carol was predeceased by parents George and Elizabeth Vogel of Sarasota; her beloved husband, Ralph Cote; her stepson, Christopher Cote; and her sister and brother-in-law, Whitney and Ray Armstrong of Manasquan, New Jersey. Above all, Carol cherished her family. She is survived by her sister, Elizabeth “Bitsy” Graham, and her husband, Tim Graham, of Ashland, Massachusetts; her daughter, Erin Mahan, and her longtime partner, Andrew Brittain; her son, Greg Mahan; her grandchildren, Matthew Mahan and Nora Mahan; her stepchildren and their spouses, Donna and John Gaumond, Michelle and Ken Adams, David and Betsy Cote, Doug and Jennifer Cote, Lisa Cote, Paul and Paula Richard, Susan Cote Bleuel, and Laurie Cote; her 23 step-grandchildren; her 21 step-great-grandchildren; and many extended family members and dear friends, all of whom were touched by her love, generosity and wonderful sense of humor. Those who wish to honor Carol’s memory may make a donation to the Alzheimer’s Association to support research, care and hope for families affected by Alzheimer’s disease.
